title: Latency & Unit Economics: Lab Playbook for Field Claims
content:
Purpose:
This doc is a lightweight lab playbook for turning engineering bench results into field-ready performance and unit-economics claims. Audience: product marketing, field sales, technical sales engineers, and benchmarking owners. Status: working draft (use, iterate, and push concrete numbers through legal/compliance before public use).

Topline messaging guidance (one-liners for GTM):
- "Faster: p95 generation latency that reduces user wait by ~3x under customer-like traffic patterns."
- "Cheaper: unit token cost improvements of 2–4x through workload-aware batching + KV caching on common prompt patterns."
- "Predictable: dedicated capacity with burst smoothing keeps SLA percentiles stable across spikes."

Why this playbook exists (problem we solve):
- Sales needs crisp, reproducible claims that map to customer value (reduced latency translates to engagement; lower token spend maps to lower OPEX).
- Engineering bench numbers are noisy and often measured in synthetic microbenchmarks; we need a repeatable pathway to field-grade claims.

Claim taxonomy (how to phrase claims safely):
- performance claim (latency): “Redwood delivers median/95th latency of X under Y workload.”
- economics claim (cost): “Typical token spend for a Q&A conversational workload is $A per 1M tokens on Redwood’s hosted offering.”
- resilience claim: “Automatic fallback to smaller model variant keeps availability > 99.9% during GPU pressure.”
- guidance: always include test conditions, model version, prompt set, hardware region, and caching/quantization config.

Minimum evidence bundle required per claim (checklist):
- Repro script and seed inputs (linked to bench repo)
- Traffic profile (concurrency, request distribution, prompt lengths)
- Model, quant/FP config, and kernel profile used
- Hardware description (instance type or dedicated pool config)
- Aggregated metrics: latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99), throughput (tokens/sec), token cost estimate (USD per 1M tokens), tail variance (stddev of p95 across repeated runs)
- A short customer-facing blurb and a technical appendix for SRE/SEs

Recommended test matrix (start small, expand):
1) Single-route interactive chat baseline
   - Model: open-model-xxl v3 (or closest public equivalent)
   - Requests: 100k requests, distribution: 60% short (<=64 tokens), 30% medium (64–512), 10% long (512–2048)
   - Concurrency sweep: 10 / 50 / 100
   - Measurements: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, cost estimate with and without prefix caching
2) Burst-heavy mixed workload
   - 1 minute bursts at 200 RPS within a background 10 RPS
   - Observe autoscale latency recovery and fallback events
3) Cost sensitivity matrix
   - Compare: default batching vs. tuned batching; no caching vs. prefix/KV cache; FP16 vs. 8-bit quantized instance
   - Output: normalized cost per 1M tokens and throughput delta

Sample sandbox results (example numbers — use bench scripts to reproduce):
- Baseline interactive chat (concurrency 50): p95 = 120 ms, p50 = 28 ms, tokens/sec = 14k, estimated cost = $18 / 1M tokens
- Competitor A (public benchmark, same model size, hosted): p95 = 340 ms, p50 = 90 ms, tokens/sec = 5.8k, estimated cost = $46 / 1M tokens
- Tuned batch + prefix caching on Redwood: p95 = 85 ms, p50 = 22 ms, tokens/sec = 26k, estimated cost = $9 / 1M tokens
Note: numbers above are illustrative. Always run current bench to lock figures.

How to convert bench to customer-friendly proof points:
1) Choose a representative customer workload (we have common templates: chat, search-re-rank, summarization).
2) Run bench with customer prompt set and traffic profile. 3 runs minimum; median of medians for p95.
3) Produce a 1‑page claim card: claim sentence, 3 bullet proof points (latency, cost, predictable capacity), and an appendix link to the raw bench output.

Competitive checks (quick checklist for legal/competitive safety):
- Validate that competitor numbers come from public docs or reproduced using same test harness.
- Avoid absolute phrasing like “cheapest” unless accompanied by strict constraint set. Prefer “up to X lower cost vs. [competitor] on Y workload.”
- Keep competitor names in technical appendix, not headline (field ops to coordinate).

Field playbook for sales & SEs (short script + demo plan):
- Opening: "Customers tell us token spend and tail latency are the two constraints that kill ML product economics. Redwood reduces both by combining runtime batching, KV prefix caching, and smart routing."
- Quick demo: show identical prompt set to Redwood vs competitor for 20 live requests; focus on perceived latency and response continuity.
- Cost conversation: overlay a 6-month TCO projection for typical usage (50M tokens/month) showing monthly $ delta and break-even on committed capacity.
- Objection handling: "What about model parity?" -> show quality-eval pass rates (we surface eval numbers per model in the catalog) and fallback policies that preserve quality during capacity events.

Risk scenarios & guardrails (what to avoid in public claims):
- Don’t claim geographic coverage unless we’ve validated regional SLOs for that region.
- Don’t conflate quantized model cost with unquantized model quality.
- If claim relies on enterprise-only Dedicated features (e.g., reserved pools), label accordingly.

Deliverables and owners (short roadmap):
- Repeatable bench repo + seed prompts: owner = Eng Bench Team (Marco) — due 2025-02-26
- Claim card template and legal checklist: owner = PMM (Aisha) — due 2025-03-04
- Sales demo kit (recorded 3-run comparisons + script): owner = SE lead (Rina) — due 2025-03-11

Appendix: Useful phrasing bank for GTM copy (pick 1–2 per asset):
- "Redwood cuts tail latency by up to 3x on customer-style chat workloads."
- "Lower token spend through intelligent batching and caching means fewer compute cycles per active session."
- "Predictable performance under burst traffic thanks to burst-smoothing and model-fallback policies."
- "Transparent token-level cost breakdown so customers can tune for latency vs. spend."

Open questions / follow-ups (notes to self):
- Need canonical competitor bench list and repro scripts (ask competitive intelligence).
- Confirm legal on calling out specific $/1M numbers in paid marketing vs. sales-only collateral.
- Pull 3 real customer prompt sets to use as canonical templates.

Notes to bench owners: keep the test harness as close to customer environments as possible (same payload serialization, identical TLS/region routing, realistic cold-start patterns). When in doubt, over-document config so SEs can reproduce during screenshare.

End of draft.
